title: Rose's socialism and the happy life in turn-of-the-century New Orleans
summary: Rose explains his defensive view of socialism, denies art is propaganda, and says New Orleans around 1900 was a capitalist society still in ascendancy that offered a happy life.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Of course, my political attitude is a classical one in this sense. And that is that I believe that any true revolutionary socialist maintains his position on an entirely defensive basis. That is, that he assumes that the capitalist society in which we live is in a process of decline and inevitable collapse. I see the basic conflict as it exists in the world as one between capital and labor, which is certainly classical. I believe that there comes a time in the relations between capital and labor against the economic political background and it is a system in which the capitalism can no longer afford the luxury of democracy and attempts to impose its and continue its system by force rather than by the machinery or the apparent, or the machinery of an apparent democratic process. Therefore, I consider that it is absolutely essential for working people to get themselves organized, to defend themselves against the onslaughts of the offense that they can anticipate from a capitalist class in decay, in exactly the same sense as I would have recommended it to the working class of Germany, as Hitler organized capitalism to oppress the working class, and as Franco did it in Spain, and as Mussolini did it in Italy. I consider that we're going to have to face the same kind of problems here at some time and worldwide. Therefore, there is no abstract ideological consideration involved. It's merely a question of trying to prepare for the inevitable collapse of the society that we have. Now, I never, I do not and never did believe that the arts serve only as propaganda tools for politics. I believe that there is such a thing as the happy life, and that man has experienced at various times and places the circumstances of a happy life, and that it is his job in order to satisfy himself to recreate those as much as possible. Now, it happens that, to me, that those things that occurred in our history, where this kind of life was apparent, was in New Orleans at the turn of the century, and certain other places like the Paris that produced the French Impressionists. And I'm for these things, and I enjoy them. And in the same way, I suppose that Coleridge enjoyed Xanadu, though he never lived there.
Now, New Orleans was a capitalist society at the turn of the century, or would you say?

Oh, yes, of course. All society at the turn of the century virtually was capitalist society, but it was capitalist society which was still in its ascendancy, and where the opportunities for the individual to make a life for himself still existed without the oppression of an oppressive economic system.
